title: SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: SynCo: Data Synthesis Co-Training for Self-Evolving LLMs via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Self-evolving LLM agents promise to improve autonomously through continual interaction and learning, reducing their dependence on manually curated supervision. Realizing this promise requires not only updating the agent, but also evolving its training experience as its capabilities change. However, most existing pipelines rely on static datasets or separately updated synthesis models, causing previously useful tasks to become trivial while overly difficult tasks remain uninformative. This growing mismatch between agent capability and training experience limits sustained self-improvement.
To address this problem, we propose SynCo , an agentic data synthesis co-training framework for self-evolving LLMs based on multi-agent reinforcement learning. SynCo jointly optimizes two independently parameterized agents: a Synthesizer that constructs training tasks from the Reasoner’s evolving capability state, and a Reasoner that learns from the resulting experience. Each synthesized task induces multiple Reasoner rollouts whose outcomes provide complementary rewards to both agents. Correctness feedback improves the Reasoner, while task quality, answer reliability, and outcome-grounded teachability guide the Synthesizer. Their updates are fed back into subsequent synthesis rounds, allowing the task-solving policy and its training distribution to evolve together. Extensive experiments across eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SynCo substantially outperforms a broad range of existing synthetic-data methods and controlled baselines, achieving the strongest overall performance while deriving most of its gains from previously unsolved problems. GitHub: https://github.com/weiyang930/SynCo.git Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/weiyang930/SynCo 1 Introduction Large language model agents are increasingly expected to improve through interaction and accumulated experience, rather than remain bounded by a fixed collection of human-curated demonstrations ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . Yet most agent training pipelines still rely on data that is static, externally constructed, or only periodically refreshed. This creates a fundamental mismatch: agent capabilities change throughout training, while the distribution of learning experience does not ( Pahuja et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) . Tasks that were once informative may become trivial, whereas tasks far beyond the agent’s competence continue to provide little useful learning signal. The resulting misalignment between the learner and its data limits both training efficiency and sustained improvement. A genuinely self-evolving agent therefore requires not merely more synthetic data, but a source of training experience that continuously adapts to its evolving capabilities ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Yue et al., 2026 ) . Recent work has begun to address this limitation through adaptive data synthesis, weakness-driven task generation, and teacher–solver or challenger–solver co-evolution ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Yue et al., 2026 ) . These approaches adapt the training data to the current learner by regenerating, selecting, or reweighting tasks according to model failures, uncertainty, or estimated difficulty. However, an adaptive data distribution does not necessarily imply joint optimization of data synthesis and task learning. Many existing frameworks still alternate between generating tasks from a previous learner checkpoint and subsequently training the learner on the resulting data ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) . Although this enables iterative adaptation, the synthesis policy and the task policy are not optimized together from the same online interaction. Data generation therefore remains an auxiliary process around agent training rather than a learnable component of the training system itself. True mutual evolution requires jointly optimizing the experience synthesizer and the learner. Such joint training creates a coupled and non-stationary learning problem. The Synthesizer shapes the Reasoner’s optimization landscape through the tasks it generates, while each Reasoner update redefines which tasks remain useful. A task that is informative at one stage may later become trivial, whereas a nominally difficult task may still provide little supervision if the Reasoner consistently succeeds or fails. The value of synthetic data therefore cannot be judged solely by static properties such as validity, novelty, or nominal difficulty, but must be grounded in the current Reasoner’s actual interaction with the data ( Yang et al., 2026a ; Kwan et al., 2026 ) . This leads to the central question of our work: Can agentic data synthesis and task learning be formulated as a unified multi-agent reinforcement learning process in which the data-synthesis policy and the task-solving policy are jointly optimized and continuously evolve together? Answering this question requires more than connecting a generator to a learner. It requires a closed loop that integrates learner-state observation, adaptive task generation, shared interaction feedback, and online updates of both policies. To address this challenge, we propose SynCo , an agentic data synthesis co-training framework for self-evolving LLMs based on multi-agent reinforcement learning. SynCo jointly optimizes two independently parameterized agents: a Synthesizer that constructs training tasks and a Reasoner that learns from them. At each iteration, the Synthesizer observes an evolving context built from the recent synthetic data pool, the Reasoner’s empirical capability profile, and feedback from rejected tasks. It then generates a structured and verifiable task tailored to the Reasoner’s current learning needs. The Reasoner performs multiple solution rollouts, whose outcomes provide complementary learning signals to both agents. Correctness rewards improve the Reasoner, while task quality, answer reliability, and outcome-grounded teachability guide the Synthesizer. Both policies are updated online through group-relative policy optimization within the same multi-agent training process. Their updates define the next synthesis round: the improved Reasoner induces a new capability state, and the improved Synthesizer converts that state into a new training distribution. Through this closed loop, SynCo enables the task-solving policy and its training data to evolve together. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We formulate agentic data synthesis and task learning as a coupled multi-agent reinforcement learning problem, and propose SynCo to jointly optimize a Synthesizer and a Reasoner within a unified online training process. • We develop a closed-loop self-evolution framework in which the Synthesizer continually adapts the training distribution to the evolving Reasoner, while outcome-grounded interaction feedback from the Reasoner directly supervises the synthesis policy. • Extensive experiments across diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that SynCo consistently outperforms a frozen-Synthesizer baseline, with most gains arising from previously unsolved problems. 2 Related Work Synthetic data has become central to LLM post-training, ranging from instruction bootstrapping methods such as Self-Instruct ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and WizardLM ( Xu et al., 2024 ) to reasoning-oriented pipelines such as STaR ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ) , MetaMath ( Yu et al., 2023 ) , and DeepSeekMath ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Recent work further improves realism, diversity, verifiability, and learner relevance: MATRIX ( Tang et al., 2025 ) generates scenarios through multi-agent simulation, FAC Synthesis ( Li et al., 2026a ) targets missing representation-space features, Explorer ( Pahuja et al., 2025 ) synthesizes trajectories through environment exploration, and SwS ( Liang et al., 2026 ) constructs problems around persistent learner weaknesses. Related pipelines extend synthetic supervision to mathematical reasoning, tool use, web interaction, and executable environments ( Gou et al., 2024 ; Ramrakhya et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . Most of these approaches nevertheless construct an offline corpus or adapt generation separately from downstream policy optimization. Self-evolving frameworks more directly couple experience generation with learner improvement. R-Zero ( Huang et al., 2025 ) , Socratic-Zero ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , and Agent0 ( Xia et al., 2025 ) establish co-evolving proposer, teacher, or curriculum roles for autonomous reasoning improvement. Dr. Zero ( Yue et al., 2026 ) and SCOPE ( Kwan et al., 2026 ) extend this paradigm to multi-turn search and open-ended document-grounded tasks, while CoEvolve ( Yang et al., 2026a ) adapts tool-use task distributions using rollout-derived forgetting and uncertainty signals. Agent-World ( Dong et al., 2026 ) , SEAD ( Dai et al., 2026 ) , AgentEvolver ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) , EvolveR ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and EvoFSM ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) further explore the evolution of environments, curricula, memories, experiences, and agent workflows. A comprehensive discussion of synthetic-data generation and self-evolving agents is provided in Appendix.A. 3 Method In this section, we present SynCo , a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that jointly optimizes agentic data synthesis and task reasoning for continual self-evolution. The overall framework is illustrated in Figure 1 . Figure 1: Overview of SynCo , a closed-loop framework for self-evolving LLMs. (1) A Synthesizer first generates capability-guided and verifiable tasks from the current learning context. (2) The resulting interaction batch is then used to jointly update the Synthesizer and the Reasoner through online multi-agent co-training. (3) The updated agents in turn reshape the future curriculum and task distribution, forming an agent–data self-evolution loop. 3.1 Problem Formulation: Agentic Data Synthesis Co-Training We consider two independently parameterized agents: a Synthesizer π S ​ ( ⋅ , θ S ) \pi_{S}(\cdot;\theta_{S}) that generates training tasks and a Reasoner π R ​ ( ⋅ , θ R ) \pi_{R}(\cdot;\theta_{R}) that learns to solve them. The Synthesizer determines the Reasoner’s training experience, while the Reasoner’s realized behavior provides feedback for improving synthesis.
